scenes.heading: Homeostasis basics
scenes.sub: How does your body stay steady on a 40 °C day?
scenes.say: Whether you're in an air-conditioned classroom or running on a forty degree day, your body keeps its temperature, water and blood sugar fairly steady. That balancing act is called homeostasis.
scenes.caption: Whether you're in an air-conditioned classroom or running on a 40 °C day, your body keeps its temperature, water and blood sugar fairly steady. That balancing act is called homeostasis.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Cruise control speeds up uphill and eases off downhill
scenes.science: Negative feedback reverses a change, back towards the set point
scenes.breaks: a car has one sensor and one control system; the body uses many receptors, plus nerves and hormones, and several effectors at once.
scenes.say: Think of cruise control set at one hundred kilometres an hour. Going uphill, the car slows, a sensor notices, and the engine gives more power. The response always works against the change. That's negative feedback. Negative means it reverses the change, not that it's bad.
scenes.caption: Think of cruise control set at 100 km/h. Going uphill, the car slows, a sensor notices, and the engine gives more power. The response always works against the change. That's negative feedback. Negative means it reverses the change, not that it's bad.

scenes.heading: Stimulus–response model
steps: Control centre: compares to set point
scenes.say: Remember: Silly Rabbits Can Eat Radishes. Stimulus, receptor, control centre, effector, response. The control centre is often the hypothalamus in your brain.

scenes.heading: Controlling temperature
scenes.say: When you're too hot, you sweat more and skin blood vessels widen to lose heat. When you're too cold, you shiver, vessels narrow to keep heat, and hairs stand up. Dilate means lose heat. Constrict means keep heat.

scenes.heading: Blood glucose
scenes.say: The pancreas controls blood glucose with two hormones. After a meal, insulin makes cells take in glucose and the liver store it as glycogen. Glucagon is released when glucose is gone: the liver breaks glycogen back down. Glucagon is the hormone, glycogen is the store.

scenes.heading: Diabetes
points: Type 1: pancreas makes little or no insulin
Managed with insulin injections or pumps
Type 2: cells stop responding to insulin
Managed with diet, exercise and medication
scenes.say: In type one diabetes, the pancreas makes little or no insulin, so blood glucose stays high. It's managed with insulin injections or pumps. In type two, cells stop responding properly to insulin.

scenes.heading: Nerves vs hormones
scenes.say: Nerves are like a phone call: fast, short and targeted, like pulling your hand off a hot plate. Hormones are like a social media post: slower, longer lasting and seen widely, but only cells with the right receptors respond.

points: Homeostasis keeps conditions in a narrow range
Stimulus, receptor, control centre, effector, response
Insulin lowers glucose; glucagon raises it
Nerves fast and short; hormones slow and long
scenes.say: Quick recap. Homeostasis keeps conditions steady so enzymes work well. Negative feedback reverses changes. Insulin lowers blood glucose and glucagon raises it. Now try the practice questions!
